title: Subsets II
description: Brute force to optimized: bitmask generation with post-hoc deduplication versus sort-first backtracking with a sibling-skip rule.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums that may contain duplicates, return all possible unique subsets (the power set), with no duplicate subset appearing more than once in the result. Subsets may be returned in any order.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"All subsets\" plus \"array may contain duplicates\" plus \"no duplicate subsets in the result\"","Backtracking with sorting first, then skipping repeated values at the same recursion depth"],["A close variant of the classic Subsets problem, but with duplicates","The \"sort, then skip equal siblings\" duplicate-avoidance technique common across backtracking problems"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Without duplicate values, every subset built by backtracking would already be unique. With duplicates present, however, choosing "the first 2" versus "the second 2" (when two equal values sit at different positions) can otherwise produce the identical subset twice; the challenge is avoiding this without an explicit deduplication step at the end.

blocks.title: Analogy: Choosing Snacks with Two Identical Cookies
blocks.text: Picture a snack tray with one apple and two identical cookies. Choosing "the first cookie" versus "the second cookie" (but not the apple) results in the exact same selection: one cookie. This problem asks for every distinct kind of selection, not every distinct sequence of picks.

blocks.caption: Sorting first groups equal values together, so duplicates can be skipped as siblings at the same recursion depth

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: nums = [1, 2, 2]
Result: [] [1] [1,2] [1,2,2] [2] [2,2]. Note there is only one [2] and one [2,2], not duplicated despite two 2's in the input.
5. How Should We Think?

Before generating subsets and deduplicating afterward, notice that sorting the array first groups equal values adjacently, which lets the recursion directly skip re-choosing an equal value as a SIBLING choice at the same level, preventing duplicate subsets from ever being generated in the first place.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every recursive call in a standard subset-backtracking template already represents a valid subset (the path built so far), so the difficulty is purely about avoiding generating the SAME subset multiple times through different choice sequences.

Observation 2: If nums is sorted first, equal values become adjacent, so whenever a choice at some recursive level considers index i, and nums[i] equals nums[i-1] where i-1 was ALSO a valid choice at this same level (i.e., i is not the very first option tried at this depth), skipping it avoids re-deriving an identical subset that a different, earlier equal element already produced.

Observation 3: This "skip if it equals the previous option at the same recursion depth" check must only compare against SIBLING choices (same start position sweep), not against ancestors deeper or shallower in the recursion.

Observation 4: Because subsets are recorded at EVERY recursive call (not just at a base case), the check must be applied inside the loop over candidate next elements, before recursing.

This leads to: sort nums first, then backtrack normally (choosing to include each candidate element from the current start position onward), but skip any candidate that equals the immediately preceding candidate already tried at the same recursion depth.
6. Brute Force Solution
Generate every subset as if all elements were distinct (using bitmasking or standard subset backtracking), then deduplicate the results using a set keyed by the sorted subset content.
Step by step algorithm

items: Generate all 2^n subsets using any standard subset-enumeration technique (bitmask or backtracking), treating positions as distinct even if values repeat.
For each generated subset, sort it and convert it to a string or tuple key.
Add it to the result only if that key has not been seen before.

codes.python:
def subsets_with_dup_brute(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    seen = set()
    result = []
    for mask in range(1 << n):
        subset = [nums[i] for i in range(n) if mask & (1 << i)]
        key = tuple(sorted(subset))
        if key not in seen:                          # deduplicate after generating
            seen.add(key)
            result.append(subset)
    return result

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Bitmasking enumerates all 2^n position-based subsets, then a set filters out those that are content-duplicates of an earlier one.
This wastes work generating subsets that will just be thrown away, and requires sorting/hashing every single subset.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2^n times n log n), generating 2^n subsets and sorting/hashing each.
Space: O(2^n times n) for the seen set and result.

Limitation: generating duplicate subsets and then discarding them is unnecessary; sorting nums first and skipping equal sibling choices during backtracking avoids ever generating a duplicate subset in the first place.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why post-hoc deduplication is wasteful: many of the 2^n bitmask-generated subsets are exact duplicates of each other whenever nums has repeated values, and discovering this only after generating and sorting each one wastes significant work.

The key structural fix: sort nums first, so equal values become adjacent. Then, within the loop that tries each candidate next element at a given recursion depth, skip a candidate if it equals the immediately previous candidate ALREADY TRIED at that same depth (not just anywhere in the array).

Why this specific skip rule is correct: it does not forbid using duplicate values altogether (subsets like [2,2] must still be generated); it only forbids using an equal value as an ALTERNATIVE first-choice at the same recursion level, since that alternative would just re-derive a subset already covered by the first equal value's branch.

The core idea: sort first, then backtrack with the sibling-skip rule, generating each unique subset exactly once directly.

Sort nums. Backtrack from a starting index: record the current path as a subset immediately, then for each candidate index from start onward, skip it if it repeats the immediately previous candidate at this same depth, otherwise include it, recurse, and undo.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for nums = [1, 2, 2] (sorted, unchanged here)

blocks.caption: Sort first, then skip a candidate that repeats the previous SIBLING candidate at the same recursion depth

codes.python:
def subsets_with_dup(nums):
    nums.sort()
    result = []
    path = []

    def backtrack(start):
        result.append(path[:])                            # every call is a valid subset
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:        # skip duplicate sibling
                continue
            path.append(nums[i])
            backtrack(i + 1)
            path.pop()                                       # undo

    backtrack(0)
    return result

blocks.text: Why This Works

Sorting first ensures every group of equal values is contiguous. Within the loop over candidate next elements at a given recursion depth, skipping a candidate whenever it equals the immediately preceding SIBLING candidate (not an ancestor) means only the FIRST occurrence of any repeated value is ever chosen as a "fresh" branch at that depth; later equal occurrences are only ever included as part of the branch already started by the first one. This guarantees every unique subset is generated exactly once, directly, with no post-processing needed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2^n times n), each of the (at most 2^n) unique subsets costs O(n) to copy.
Space: O(n) recursion depth (excluding output).

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Subsets II demonstrates the general "sort first, then skip equal sibling choices at the same recursion depth" technique for avoiding duplicate results in backtracking, applicable whenever the input may contain repeated values.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to sort nums first, which breaks the sibling-skip check (equal values must be adjacent for it to work correctly).
Comparing against the wrong index, using i > 0 instead of i > start, which would incorrectly forbid using a repeated value within the SAME branch (as a child), not just as a sibling.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["All elements identical","Only n+1 unique subsets exist (one for each possible count of the repeated value, from 0 to n)."],["No duplicate values at all","Behaves identically to the standard Subsets problem, 2^n unique subsets."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explaining precisely why "i > start" (not "i > 0") is the correct condition, since it distinguishes sibling choices at the current depth from valid parent-child repeated selections, shows precise understanding of the technique.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "the input may contain duplicates, avoid duplicate results", think: sort first, then skip a candidate equal to the previous SIBLING candidate at the same recursion depth.
Interview Follow-up Questions

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The bitmask-plus-dedup approach runs in O(2^n times n log n) time and O(2^n times n) space; the sort-plus-sibling-skip backtracking approach runs in O(2^n times n) time and O(n) extra space (excluding output).
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: sort first, then backtrack with a sibling-skip rule to avoid duplicate subsets.

Core Idea: record every recursive call as a valid subset; when choosing the next element to include, skip any candidate equal to the immediately preceding SIBLING candidate already tried at the same depth.
Time: O(2^n times n log n) for the brute force, O(2^n times n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(2^n times n) versus O(n) extra (excluding output).
Most Important Observation: sorting groups duplicates together, letting a simple sibling-skip check prevent duplicate subsets directly, with no post-processing needed.
Interview Difficulty: a standard, widely applicable duplicate-avoidance technique in backtracking.
One line memory trick: sort first, then skip a repeated sibling choice at the same recursion depth.
